utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin and Ekkehard Withopf. We will be joined by the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Mr. Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and everyone who ensures that these proceedings run smoothly. We'll be hearing a witness today, but before we commence with the examination, there are a few issues that we should deal with before. First of all, as you are aware, the Trial Chamber has rendered a decision with regard to modifying the list of witnesses and exhibits. As far as I can remember, in this decision I indicated that the Trial Chamber would take a separate decision with regard to the expert witness's report, General Reinhardt. This concerned document 108 which was included in the Prosecution's list. Document exhibit 108 followed on 107 documents which were provided to General Reinhardt so he could use them when preparing his report. There is a difficulty that remains if the Trial Chamber is to render a decision with regard to document 108, and this concerns an ambiguity with regard to the report of General Reinhardt. In a paragraph -- I think it's paragraph 2 -- it is indicated that he received additional documents from the Prosecution. Do these additional documents -- are they included in the 107 documents that were provided to him, or are these additional documents not included among the 107 documents? I would appreciate it if the Prosecution could inform me of whether all the documents provided to General Reinhardt are the 107 documents listed and whether the paragraph that relates to the document and concerns additional documents. Could I be told whether these additional documents are in fact an integral part of the 107 documents provided to him. Perhaps the Prosecution cannot answer me immediately, but this is my question and I would like to have a response as soon as possible before we hand down our decision concerning document 108. The second issue has to do with documents that were on stand-by yesterday and were given a number for -- were marked for identification. Could the Prosecution tell me what they have to say about the documents which were put forward by the Defence yesterday and that were marked for identification. Are there any objections that the Prosecution would like to raise today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, after we got forwarded the one document we asked the Defence for Mr. Kubura for, we have no objections to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are no objections. Could Mr. Registrar give me all the documents that were marked for identification so that we can give these documents a definitive number today -- definitive numbers today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a pity that we don't have a red and green light in the courtroom to indicate whether we're in open session or in private session. It would make it easier to follow the proceedings. It's an idea that I'm suggesting to the registrar. Naturally, it's marked on the screen, but then we have to have a look at the screen, at the computer screen. If we had a light in front of us, it would be a lot simpler, as is the case when there's a radio or television broadcast there is an indication saying when one is on air. That would have made things a lot simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Can you hear what I am saying interpreted into your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You'll be testifying before this Tribunal. I must first ask you what your first and last name are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Nenad Bogeljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd of August, 1963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kakanj, in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Odranska 4, Sisak, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a telecommunications engineer and I work for the Croatian telecommunications centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you're going to be examined here, you're going to testify as a witness, but you must first take the solemn declaration that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Witness, as I have said, you'll be testifying before this Chamber. The Prosecution will ask you some questions; they are to your right. After the Prosecution have concluded its examination, Defence counsel for the accused, who are to your left, will also ask you some questions. The Judges, who are before you, may at any time ask you questions in order to clarify issues that require clarification. I would be grateful if you could answer the questions as extensively as possible. If there are any questions that you do not understand, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. I would also like to inform you that as you have taken the solemn declaration and you have sworn to tell the truth, you must not give false testimony. If you do, proceedings may be instituted against you for false testimony. And if within the framework of your testimony -- if while testifying there might be something you could say that could incriminate you for some crime, you should inform me of this so that we can guarantee or so that we can assure you that what you say cannot be used against you. Have you understood everything I have told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now ask the Prosecution to start their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogeljic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, you just informed the Trial Chamber that you were born in Kakanj. Can you please also inform us where you grew up.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: In Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Bogeljic, when you joined the JNA? And if so, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: From the 6th of October, 1983, until September/October 1994. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There is written in the transcript "September/October 1994." Mr. Bogeljic, can you please clarify this. Was it 1994 or 1984?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No, no, 1984. 1984. It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was living in Kakanj, but I worked in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And since when did you work in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I started working after I'd finished my schooling. I graduated in May or June -- in May, and I started working on the 29th of December, 1986, in Zenica for the PTT, the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Are you married, Mr. Bogeljic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the ethnic background of your wife.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: She is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what's your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In 1992 in Zenica, how would you describe the relation between the Muslims and the Croats in Zenica in 1992 and in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, everything was different from what it was like in 1989. There was some sort of confrontations. The JNA arrived in Zenica. They came from Slovenia and Croatia; that is to say, they came from Karlovac. The Serbs went to the barracks. The Muslims and Croats were together then. There were no problems of any kind. In 1992, these confrontations started. There were problems concerning weapons, as far as I could tell. Various armies were formed and so on. Until 1993, I personally didn't have any problems. I went to work as usual until March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would you please stop there.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That's when it started --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, you were referring that in 1992 these confrontations started. Which confrontations are you referring to? Confrontations between who?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, between the HVO - they were on one side - and various forces, various Bosniak forces. At the time, the BH Army hadn't been organised. There was the Territorial Defence and some sort of Muslim league that had been formed in Kakanj. There were the Green Berets. There were a number of formations. And then gradually there was increasing intolerance among the people. Not among the ordinary people. Someone provoked this. But things became very tense in Bosnia. We say it was like a pressure cooker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Bogeljic, when you noticed foreigners in the area of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the Zenica TK centre. That's what it was called then, and it's still called the same now. And it was the PTT, but I was an engineer, so I worked in the part that had to do with telecommunications. And I would travel from Kakanj to work in Zenica on a daily basis. And from 1993 and perhaps even 1992, but from 1993 for sure, I would frequently see people who couldn't speak our language, the language that's spoken in Bosnia. They would travel around by bus, and quite a lot of them could even speak our language quite well. But everyone in my company were aware of this fact, the people who were with me on a daily basis. They were aware of the fact that these people were from Arab countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These people from Arab countries, did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Those that I saw - because the bus was going from Zenica towards Visoko, and I got off at Kakanj, not every day but occasionally - I would see them wearing green wind jackets. It wasn't the traditional standard uniform, but I could see that they spoke differently and they had a different colour of their skin, though there are some people in our own country in Bosnia who are dark. But they wear shorter hair. I didn't communicate with them, but I would see them often at the bus stop or in the bus. I had no problems with them, I personally. They were simply travelling by bus like all the rest of us. They weren't causing any problems then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These people you are referring to, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, they didn't carry long barrels. I remember one man, whom I saw several times -- as I was saying, I commuted every day until March 1993 -- he was quite short. And once I saw that he had a pistol under his jacket. But I never saw long-barrelled weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were there any other such individuals from Arab countries which had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, around town in 1993 one could come across them, but I saw people in the bus. However, my friends who worked with me - and I talked to them on a daily basis - they told me that they had a camp somewhere at Vjetrenice, a training camp. I never went there, so I didn't see it during the conflict. I did before, because I used to work in telecom and then I travelled all over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you get to know about a further location where these Arabs from foreign countries were based at the time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I also heard that there was a camp at Rostovo. My cousin was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And are you aware, Mr. Bogeljic, whether the Arabs from foreign countries were also based in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I heard - I didn't see this; that's a fact - that there were some at the music school. People were talking about that. I would move around Zenica, but I can't claim that there were people there. What I do know for certain is what I saw, and I saw them in the bus and at the bus stop and that these were persons definitely from other countries. Now, how numerous they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Bogeljic, as to when roughly you for the first time got to know that the foreigners from Arab countries were at the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, but sometime in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it more at the beginning of 1993 or more in the middle or more towards the end?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have to object. The witness, in answer to several questions from the Prosecutor, said that he only heard from others, that others had told him, that he himself never saw such things. And in spite of such an answer by the witness, the Prosecutor repeatedly is asking about what the witness heard, though he didn't lay the ground for putting hearsay questions to the witness. So could the Prosecutor be cautioned that he cannot continue this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I disagree with the objection made by my learned colleague. Hearsay evidence is admissible; it's only an issue about the evidentiary value and the weight of the evidence. The witness has said that he got to know from friends about these facts. I laid the ground to ask the questions which I asked, namely, as to when and from whom he got to know and at what point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the facts recounted by the witness on the basis of hearsay, it needs to be specified how he gathered that information, at what point in time, and who told him. As you both know, the facts conveyed on the basis of hearsay are admissible, but on condition that we know exactly the context and the source. We cannot accept hearsay evidence without any basis, any groundwork. So if, Witness, you were told that these foreigners arrived on such-and-such a date, you have to tell us who told you, when, and under what circumstances so that we can appreciate the value of what you're telling us. I give the floor to the Prosecutor to try and clarify this point which has been objected to by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And that was exactly what I was trying to do prior to my learned colleague making her objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber as from whom you got to know that Arabs from foreign countries were in the Zenica Music School.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, I went to work every day. And in Zenica in my company there were quite a number of Muslims working there -- or let me correct myself, Bosniaks. Zenica had a majority Bosniak population, but there were a large number of Croats and Serbs and we were working together. And then somebody would be living close to the music school and he would say that he saw these people entering, but I can't tell you the name of that person. But everyone in Zenica knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You just said prior to the objection of my learned colleague that you got to learn about foreigners from Arab countries in the Zenica Music School in early 1993. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to -- as from whom you got to know this.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: At work we spoke about this. All I can say is the names of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people working with me, but I can't tell you exactly which one of them told me this. People were walking around Zenica. They lived in various parts of Zenica. They lived in Tetovo, where the camps were. Then in the music school people were detained and they said that they saw people there. But I didn't go there. I can't say that I saw it. But I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Bogeljic, to Kakanj. Can you please describe for the information of the Trial Chamber the situation in the second half of 1992 and in early 1993 in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to remember all these things because it was a long time ago, but I shall try to summarise everything. As regards life in Kakanj municipality itself, I think that the conflicts spread to Kakanj very late. I think that the coexistence between us Croats and Bosniaks in Kakanj was always very good and we never had any problems or conflicts between us and the Bosniaks. There were far fewer Serbs. The Bosniaks and Croats constituted about half the population. There was 50/50 per cent. There are many mixed marriages in Kakanj. My mother [as interpreted] is married to a Bosniak; I am married to a Serb. And before we had absolutely no problems, until politics gained the upper hand. And then what happened -- we all know happened, contrary to what we needed. We all know that now. The conflict started in such a way that both on the Bosniak and on the Croatian side - at least, that is my opinion - people came to power in the municipality and in the army, people who shouldn't have been there, who shouldn't have held those positions. Those conflicts could easily have spared Kakanj. On the Bosnian side --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, may I please stop you there. In early 1993, can you please inform the Trial Chamber which military units of which armies were based in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: On the Croatian side -- or rather, the Croatian people had a component known as the HVO. There had been attempts to form something called HOS in Kakanj, but it never succeeded. Similarly, on the Bosniak side at first there was this green legion, then the Green Berets, then of course the Territorial Defence, which was the first. However, we Croats did not fear the Territorial Defence. One of my friends who studied with me was one of the commanders, and he helped me leave Kakanj. However, then this 7th Muslim came to Kakanj. I don't wish to say that they are the only ones to blame. I think that everyone is to blame and that this shouldn't have happened at all, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade, when did they come to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I am unable to tell you exactly because I don't know. I was never a soldier. I was not interested in politics, but my wife has a house very close to the motel and her whole family lives close to the motel. And all the Bosniaks living near the motel know me and I know them. And I know that the Croatian component in the municipality did not agree with the accommodation of that unit at the motel. I heard this from people who were in the authorities, who were involved in politics. But this could have been at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware whether at the beginning of 1993 a military unit was based in the building which is known as the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. A battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I know that for certain, because I myself had some problems with them, some unpleasantness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown via Sanction the Prosecution Exhibit P10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform us what you can see on the photograph in front of you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: It is the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the Motel Sretno in which at the beginning of 1993 the 7th Muslim Brigade was based?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bogeljic, how did you get to know that it was the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Everyone in Kakanj knew it. We saw them. We saw soldiers with the insignia, various insignia. There were some with various patches. But anyway, my wife and myself went to the railway station when I was going by bus or by train - though I mostly took the bus because I lived in a part of town that is a little further away from the railway station, so it was more difficult for me to go there - but we would see them on a daily basis. We saw them disarming the Serb population there, because the Serbs had weapons they had received from the SDS. They even offered my father-in-law a weapon, which I found difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, you're referring to various military insignia. Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber how these insignia looked like.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: So many years after the events, I have forgotten many things. But some things are still imprinted in one's mind. I saw insignia with some Arabic letters and some sort of a sword like those from Turkish times, from Ottoman times. Others had on their sleeves "Allah-U-Ekber," a crescent and a star. Some wore bandannas and the men who took me in had these bandannas with Arabic letters on them. So it is difficult to remember all the details, but there is no doubt that a battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was there. There's no doubt about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, I'm now going to show you a photo board with a number of military insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the Prosecution Exhibit P4 via the Sanction technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, you have in front of you a photo board with a number of military insignia. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber which one or which ones, if any, you have seen in the context of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the Motel Sretno in 1993. If you please could make reference to the number of the respective photo board -- insignia.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Should I just tell you what I saw at the Sretno Motel or all the insignia I ever saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The ones you've seen at the Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Number 1 I think I saw. I also think I saw number 24, and numbers 9 and 12. Number 9 I saw, I think -- I think that the patch under number 9 was placed later, when the 7th Muslim Brigade was integrated within the BH Army and came under its command, whereas the patch under number 12 was worn by the regular troops of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whereas members of the 7th Muslim Brigade also wore the army patch, but later on when they came under their command. I think that's how it was. There were different patches. Most of these are familiar, except for the Serb ones, because you couldn't see them in our parts of the country. But most of the others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogeljic. Moving on to a different subject. Did you, Mr. Bogeljic, ever join the HVO or did you ever work for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: In March 1993, it was very awkward, all these events happening in Central Bosnia. In one town, the Bosniaks were the victims; in another, the Croats. As it was difficult for the Bosniaks in towns with a majority Croat population, so it was difficult for us in the other -- in the opposite situation. And various brigades were formed. I saw in Zenica, in Radakovo, when brigades were being formed lined up. There were very many troops in towns. People were victimised, and we too were exposed to such danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, please listen very carefully to the questions. The question was: Did you ever join the HVO or did you ever support the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I was going to go on and tell you that when you interrupted me. In 1993 -- I can even tell you the exact date when I realised that my safety was no longer secure in Zenica. Everyone felt the same, and I simply asked my manager and told him that I would leave, because one of my colleagues, who was working with me, said that I was tapping some conversations, which was absolutely untrue. My superior said that he didn't believe it, but I said that I wouldn't stay on. I think sometime in mid-March I stopped working, and I worked in the HVO. I wasn't a soldier. I wasn't armed. I was simply there as a technical person who had some knowledge of mobile telephones. And the inhabitants of Kakanj know this: I installed with the help of a colleague of mine a couple of mobile NMT-technology devices. This is analogous mobile telephones, and we install them in several places for communication purposes. Everyone used these facilities, both Bosniak, Croats, and Serbs, all the inhabitants of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, did you ever wear an HVO uniform during this time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Bogeljic, when you have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to tell you about this. I was physically taken away from my family. I was deprived of my liberty. Now, whether that is an arrest -- for me, an arrest, when you're accused of something and you're taken away by the police. But this was under force of arms. A man was standing there, threatening to throw a grenade at my mother-in-law when they took me in and took me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when this happened. Do you recall the exact date?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I remember. Of course I remember. On the 18th of May, 1993, I think it was about half past 4.00. Members of the army - that is, the 7th Muslim Brigade - that were in the motel came and they were arresting people who were in the houses around the motel and the settlement of Povezice. I just happened to be there. I was in the neighbourhood visiting my cousin who was in a Serb house. The brother of the man who had abandoned the house gave her the keys to live there, and this was near the railway station. And by chance I went back to fetch some cigarettes. I was still smoking at the time. And my mother-in-law waved her hand to tell me to get away, but I didn't understand what she meant and I came in. And I saw soldiers there. They had -- told me they had a search warrant. I didn't take it seriously. I said, "What for? What do you mean?" And they said that they had information that my father-in-law had some weapons in his house and some money. The house had already been searched, and everything was scattered all over the place. They didn't say anything nasty to me, except that they had their rifles at the ready. And they told me that they hadn't found anything in the house, and then they left. Ten minutes later I went to fetch my wife to clean up the mess. They came back, however, four or five of them. One stood to the side. My mother-in-law was not very mobile. She pointed a gun at her [as interpreted]. And he said if she moves he would shoot. And then they opened the garage. I think somebody must have sent a report. Apparently they wanted to search the garage and the cars. I wasn't watching. Someone came out -- one of them came out and said that he had found a box with bullets, and he asked me where the rifle was. I said I knew nothing about a rifle. I was never a soldier except in the former JNA. And then some insults were hurled at me. One swore my Serb mother. I said I wasn't a Serb. Then he said, "That's even worse." He cursed my Ustasha mother. These were people I didn't know. They had come from somewhere else, maybe from the surrounding villages or something like that. I didn't know them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, may I stop you there, please. Once you have been arrested by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade on the 18th of May, 1993, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: They took me to the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the Motel Sretno, where in the Motel Sretno were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the Motel Sretno very well now, but I entered the motel. That's the place where they would celebrate the new year and other festive occasions, marriages, et cetera; weddings, et cetera. So I know what it looks like. They took me in. You have the reception to the right; to the left, there is a restaurant or a hall of some kind; when you go straight ahead, there is a cloakroom. When they took me in, there were some troops. I don't know exactly. There was confusion. Insults were hurled around. I was pushed around. No one asked me about weapons any more. All they wanted was money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The troops you'd seen in the reception area, which military unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I think they were all members of the 7th Muslim. To be quite frank and precise, when I answered the motel I knew what to expect. I didn't even pay attention to details. I tried to defend myself. I said I worked in the TK centre in Zenica. I said I'd helped a lot with the communications for the BH Army. And then they asked me, "Are you helping the Muslims?" So there was nothing you could say to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: From the reception area, where were you brought to afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: They took me outside. They said they'd kill me if I didn't tell them where the money was. I didn't know what money they were referring to. I had something in my wallet, and my wife told these people who took me away -- or, rather, I gave -- I handed my wallet over and she returned it because they took everything that they found in the house, everything that was of value. And then when I arrived there, I still had my wallet on me. They took it, and I think they were about -- there were about 1.900 German marks in it. We had some savings and everything was kept in one place. Naturally, they took that. They asked me if I had any over money, and I said, "Leave me alone. I have some money in Catici," which is where my parents live. "Let me go, and I will give you everything I have." But naturally, they didn't release me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were taken outside. After you were taken outside the Motel Sretno, where to were you taken?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: On the other side, to the flank, well, you have the main road from Kakanj to Zenica there. It heads towards the crossroads. So on the side there's an entrance down below. I'd never used it before. I'd used the upper entrance. I'd passed by the reception and go to where we would have coffee and socialise. But there is a warehouse down there and a number of rooms. There is a large room that they took me to. And opposite the motel there is a house. Local Muslims -- local Bosniaks lived there. They knew me, and I know that one woman said, "Let the young man go. I know him." His son had gone to secondary school with me in Sarajevo. Not the same secondary school, but we'd travelling to. And then one of the soldiers said, "Move or I'll kill you," and then they took me inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, I'm now going to show you a further photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It will be a new photograph. It will be shown via Sanction. And the Prosecution has the respective numbers of paper copies available for the Defence and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, do you see the photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the area -- or what can you actually see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: From the upper side, where you have this container, the entrance to the motel is 10 metres to the left, if I can see everything well. They took me from there and took me into this room straight ahead. We call this a sort of antechamber. There's a warehouse down there, and there are a number of rooms there. I was in a number of them, so I can remember this. But I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, can I please stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with a black texter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please mark on the paper copy of the photograph where to you were brought on that day. Can you just mark the entrance, please.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Can I do it with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You can mark it with an "X" or an arrow, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please, Mr. Bogeljic, write "This is the entrance to the area where I was brought to."

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it should be put on the ELMO, because we only have the Sanction image and we can't see what the witness is pointing to. It would be good if we could follow too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us what you have written down on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: "That's the entrance they took me to the building through on that day."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please date and sign this photograph, sign it with your name, please, and today is the 28th of January, 2004.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want to tender this into evidence? Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution wishes to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bogeljic, I'm now going to show you a further photograph. It's again a new photograph. We have the respective numbers of hard copies available. Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on the photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That's the entrance into the building. The bags -- the sacks that you can see inside, they weren't there at the time. I spent about 45 minutes in there. I was tortured for about 45 minutes. It was terrible. I was beaten too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic --

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Behind the sacks, I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there. Is this the entrance to the area where you were brought to, the area of the Motel Sretno? And can you please answer with either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with a hard copy, and can the witness please sign it and date it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, once you were brought to this area behind the entrance door, the rear entrance door of the Motel Sretno, what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Nothing very nice. It's difficult for me to remember all of those events. I think it was about half past 4.00 when I arrived, and at quarter to 5.00 - I remember this well - I entered this area. I know that was the time because I had a watch on me which was broken when they were beating me. I also had a gold chain, which I still have - it's a souvenir - at one point in time this was broken off. It lasted from quarter to 5.00 to half past 5.00, about 45 minutes, roughly speaking. These are beatings which it's very difficult to support. They would beat me with their rifles. They would kick me. They would beat me with wooden planks, whatever they could get their hands on. There were four or five of them. And this went on until, well, let's say, about half past 5.00. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would you please, prior to continuing, inform the Trial Chamber who actually beat you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were in the motel, in this unhappy hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to what army did these soldiers belong to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, they were the same people who had brought me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: The same people who had taken me to the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right. Can you please continue in detailing the further beatings, if any, that were inflicted to you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, the torture was terrible. During those 30 minutes, they broke several of my ribs. I know exactly what sort of wounds, what sort of injuries I had after the torture. But when I went into another room -- well, what I've been speaking about lasted for over half an hour, 45 minutes. It's difficult to remember everything. It's difficult to remember all of them. I didn't even see the people there. They would just trample on you and hit you with their rifle butts. But when someone brought a police truncheon, that was the worst part of it. They would beat me with this truncheon on my back. I asked them not to beat me in the area of my right kidney, but one of them who was beating me said, "Just beat him in the area of his right kidney."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber why you asked the soldier to not beat you in the area of your right kidney.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, because I had certain problems with that right kidney, and the problems I have with that kidney today are even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After these beatings with the different tools, were there any further beatings inflicted on you in the course of that night?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, that beating didn't really stop. It would stop when they became tired. They were beating me. They were beating me constantly. They only took me from this room, which is here in the front -- there are some stairs there. They put me on a chair there. And one of the men said that I would be hit 20 times with some sort of a wooden plank. I don't know what it was exactly. It's very difficult for me to describe this item in precise terms. And the fear I felt just can't be described. He said if I groaned, I'd be hit 50 times. Then the first time I was hit, I fell back and I hit my head against the stairs. And I think I lost consciousness for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened when you got back your consciousness?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: There was something warm on my face. I think one of them urinated on me. I still hadn't come to, not completely, you understand. It's difficult for me to think back to all those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once or after this portion of the beatings stopped, were there any further beatings in the course of that night inflicted on you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, the beating was almost continual. They would stop when the people who were beating us became tired. If you're beating someone with some sort of a big plank and your arms start aching and if you have to hold a rifle which weighs a few kilograms, you get tired. In this other room they continued to beat me. So this beating lasted from, as I have said, quarter to 5.00, roughly speaking. But at about ten to 7.00 I entered a third room, which is where the other detainees where kept, in this other room. They said that they would cut my throat. One of the soldiers brought some knives. He had a long knife which resembled a kitchen knife. But there was another one which was particular. It looked like those small Turkish knives. It was curved. And something was written on it, on the handle. And then he said, "Choose the knife you want us to cut your throat with." I said, "Don't cut my throat." I begged the man. I said, "Shoot me. I can't put up with this any more."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, Mr. Bogeljic, this threat to kill you with a knife, did you take it serious at that time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, I took the entire situation very seriously all the time. I'm a Catholic. I go to church. So at one point in time I started praying to God because I thought it was all over. It's very difficult to imagine what such a situation is like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you were making reference that you were put in a room where other detainees were in. Can you please inform us whether there were other detainees, how many, and what their ethnic background was, if you know.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. It was May -- I have to say this. It was May, and when I entered, it was very warm. I was only wearing a T-shirt and a track-suit and training shoes. When I entered, because it was dark inside, I couldn't see the people. But behind this next room, there is some sort of a metal fence. And after the first and second room, they would beat me there. I think that there is a toilet here, if I remember it correctly. I crawled and they pulled me back by my legs. After all those beatings, it was about 7.00, because I know that when I entered I didn't have the watch any more. But I found my chain on the floor later on and put it into my sock. That's why I still have it. Then I entered the room to the left. There were people inside. But as I had come in from the daylight and it was dark inside, I couldn't recognise anyone. I asked what the time was, and they were all afraid, so no one dared respond. They'd been listening to such screams or such groans for an hour and a half that they were completely scared. They didn't dare reply. Only after a while I recognised a number of people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who had studied with me in Sarajevo. I recognised -- can I mention any names? Is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If you are feeling comfortable to do so, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Afterwards, when all this had passed, I met three persons whom I didn't know before. They were three persons from Ilijas. I think the village is called Misoca. That's where the BH Army was engaged in action against the Serbian troops. They had collected them from houses up there, and in Povezice, which is a settlement near the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, may I stop you there. The question was: How many further detainees have you seen in the Motel Sretno. Can you please give us a --

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were 16 of us in total. I was the fifteenth person who entered the room, in which there were 14 people at the time. A sixteenth person was brought in later, at about half past 7.00 or 8.00. That's when the last person arrived. If this is important - I don't know if it is - 12 of them were Croats and 4 of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. These other detainees, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, one of them - I don't know the person's name - he even had some sort of a card to show that he was a -- that he had been a member of the Territorial Defence. He said that that might help him, but it didn't. All the others were civilians, as far as I know. I know some of the people because they had studied with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These other detainees, were they also beaten in the course of that night?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Everyone was beaten in the course of that night. No one was spared the beatings. When they shoved me into that room, they didn't touch them. After I had entered the room, they called out and said, "Where is that person who has the red car?" I was sitting at the back, and I didn't want to come forward. They said, "if they come to fetch you, it will be even worse." Then I approached that metal fence, and they said that I should put my head through the bars and then they started beating me over the head with a wooden plank. They did that a couple of times. And then after that, they started beating everyone else. I asked the people if anyone had beaten them, and they said that up until that time no one had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The other detainees, were they beaten to the same or to a similar extent as you have been beaten?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, the beating I was given was the worst. But in a certain sense others received more severe beatings. But everyone was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's the right point in time to have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 3.45. We'll have a 25-minute break, and we will resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, in the course of the night you have been detained in the Motel Sretno, did anybody make you say, sing, or shout something?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what were you requested to say, sing, or shout?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: After the torture that I have already described, I think some new people arrived who -- or one of them I remember very well his nickname. He said his name was Geler, and he said, "When I say 'Tekbir', all of you must as one voice say 'Allah-U-Ekber'." We didn't quite understand, and then they came in and said they would beat us even harder if we don't say that. And then they beat us, and then we repeated after them "Allah-U-Ekber," and it went on like that. This nickname that I mentioned, Geler, he had on his feet Adidas sports shoes like those worn by the police, and he said to me, "Look, this is Zivko Totic's shoes. Say hello to Dario Kordic and Tudjman and tell them Geler and still alive." I had no connection with either of them, so I didn't know what he meant. Then the beatings continued. Every 15 minutes they would come inside and beat each and every one of us. After 15 minutes, they would come back again and start beating again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, did there come a time when the beating actually stopped?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think the beating stopped after 3.00 a.m., because I think about 3.30 or 4.00 - I'm not quite sure about the time - an officer came in. He was wearing a uniform, and he said what his name was but I can't remember it. He said that all this was a misunderstanding, that it was a mistake that we were there. He asked whether anyone had beaten us. We couldn't stand on our feet, and it was quite obvious what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were your injuries at this point in time, were they visible?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Horribly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bogeljic, how did you get to know that this individual has been an officer?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, a man with any intelligence can distinguish between a foot soldier and an officer. He himself said he was an officer. As I say, I can't remember his name; it was more than ten years ago. He was 46 or 47. Let's say he was some sort of a lieutenant or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. And were you finally released?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. I would just like to point out something: Among those men who were there, there was a man. I later learnt he was also a soldier. I don't know his name. But he came from a village called Trsce, close to Kakanj. That man assisted us a lot. He brought us water and cigarettes. And they gave us dates to eat. And he told us why we were being held there. I didn't really know why they were keeping us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, once you were released, what injuries did you have, injuries which resulted from the beatings inflicted on you in the Motel Sretno during that night?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That day, with some of the men we went to the health centre in Kakanj. To be quite honest, I was afraid to go there, because I think it was my brother who was living in Kakanj and whose wife is a Bosniak. I think they took us to see a doctor and they x-rayed me. I had six broken ribs, both my kidneys had been moved. I had knife wounds in two places, a haematoma on my kidney, which is now 4 centimetres in size. And three months later I reached Croatia. I was in hospital. And then they discovered that my spine had been damaged too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your and the other detainees' injuries were videotaped?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. A day later. I think we left the motel on the 19th. On the 20th, I went to the health centre in Kakanj. And then I ended up in Haljinici, another village, where the HVO was in control. They held that part of the territory. And there was a health centre there with two doctors. One was Serb and the other was a Croat. They were married to Croats. And then a man came who used to be president of the federation, Niko Lozancic. He was a police inspector and he asked whether we would allow photographs to be taken. People were afraid. I personally, I have family. But nevertheless I said okay. And then this was videotaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, was it the day after the release?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I was released 24 hours after being taken there, and this was on the 20th. So yes, the day after my release, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were there any further victims and the injuries of any further victims videotaped?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were they videotaped on the very same day as your injuries were videotaped?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: We were all in that health centre at Haljinici on the same day. So I think that most were videotaped, except that some didn't want to show their face.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm now going to show a video sequence. This material Defence counsel have been provided with as part of the Prosecution exhibits on the 10th of October last year. I will show a sequence of four different videos, and I would like to witness to comment on these videos. I will show it via the Sanction technology and CDs with the videos on it will be provided in the course of today's session to the registry and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, there will be now a video footage -- video footage appear on the screen. Can you please carefully have a look at it. Once it's finished, I will ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber who one can see on this videotape -- on this video footage.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That is the last man who came to the motel that night. He came after the rest of us. He's from Ilijas. I knew his name. He's from Misoca, a Croat village. They were chased out by the Serbs and he came to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you, Mr. Bogeljic, a further portion of video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber whom one can see on this video footage.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I think it is the man who said that he was a member of the TO in Misoca. Anyway, that he had fought on the side of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So he's not a man from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, has this individual been with you in the Motel Sretno during the night of the 18th to the 19th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Has this person been beaten during the night he spent in the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I've already said so. They were all beaten. He's one of the sixteen who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, I'm now going to show you a third portion of video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber whom one can see on this portion of the video footage.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That man was also with me. I don't know his name. I don't know whether he's from Kakanj, but I think he was from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, he was with you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, "he was with you." Does that mean he was with you in the Motel Sretno during the night from the 18th May 1993 to the 19th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you know whether this person has been beaten during this very same night?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, I'm now going to show you a fourth portion of video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber who the person on this video footage is.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, once the CDs are available, the Prosecution wishes to tender this video footage into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The CDs will be ready when?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the CDs will be ready in the course of the today's court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, the injuries one can see on this video footage, the injuries on your body, are these injuries the result of the beatings inflicted on you in the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: All of them are the result of the beatings. All this happened at the Sretno Motel during a period of 20-odd hours. Only what we see on this videotape is nothing like what it really looked like in reality. It was much worse. That's me, only I had hair in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Other than showing your injuries to the people who took the video, did you at any occasion show your injuries to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I did. That day, when I came out of the motel, I went to a house across the road from the motel, about 100, 150 metres away. My wife's parents lived there. We went there because my wife was there, who thought I was no longer among the living. And then we went to my parents' place. They live in a village close to Kakanj called Catici. And then a couple of hours later - I can't remember exactly - Pavo Sljivic came, who was the HVO commander in Kakanj. I think it was him. I can't remember exactly. There may have been a couple of men with him. And then he asked me whether I would go with him to show this to a colonel, because there was a meeting between the BH Army and the HVO to calm down tensions, because the conflicts hadn't really started yet. I didn't really feel like going, but I went nevertheless, and we went to a meeting attended by representatives of the BH Army and the HVO and this colonel, whom I met later on, subsequently. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, please. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I entered. On one side there were three men seated. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. And then at the head of the table was the French colonel and an officer next to him and an interpreter. And on the other side, if I remember well - I don't know who exactly - but anyway, representatives of the HVO. Then Pavo Sljivic, who was the commander - I remember that well, because I don't know the other people who were there - it was a long time ago, anyway. But I do know he said, "Look, yesterday you killed one of our men and now sixteen men have almost been beaten to death." He mentioned a name. When he was speaking, he said, "Kubura, look what your men are doing. And we are negotiating a truce and covering up our trenches." I remember that well. I didn't know anyone inside. That is what I can say. But this I remember very well, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the course of this meeting, have you been asked to do anything?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember exactly when somebody said something to the effect, "Well, he's fine. Nothing's wrong with him." They had started treating me, putting something -- an ointment on my back, and - we had washed, of course - but I took off my T-shirt. And I remember very well that there was a young woman from Kakanj. She was the interpreter. And I know the woman turned her head away she was so horrified with what she saw. After that, we left. My wife was waiting in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once your took off your T-shirt in the course of this meeting, were your injuries visible to the same extent we just have seen on the video footage?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe they were even more pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was this individual which has been addressed by the HVO commander Pavo Sljivic with the name "Kubura" and with the sentence, "Kubura, look what your men are doing," has this individual seen the injuries in the course of this meeting once you took off your shirt?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Of course. Everyone saw it. They were all inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, please allow me to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This individual which has been addressed with the name of Kubura, was he an ordinary soldier or was he an officer?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty. There were three men sitting there. They were in uniform. Now, whether he was an officer or not -- because they were all seated when we walked in. And when I took off my T-shirt, I remember that Pavo Sljivic was shouting and he mentioned this name. That's all I remember. But the face, I'm afraid it is very difficult for me to say who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, after all these events, did you ever go back to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I go to Kakanj every year at least a couple of times. I was there two or three months ago. I have many friends there, people I used to work with. They come and see me. We meet on the seaside. We communicate daily by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this mean you are since then not any more living in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That is right. In October 1993, I left Bosnia and Herzegovina, as my wife is a Serb. We left via Vares. In Vares, there were some people through which you could leave. Even my brother left, whose wife is a Bosniak. He also left through the so-called Republika Srpska. I went to Belgrade, via Belgrade to Hungary, to the airport. And since my son's passport had expired, we had to go to Germany. I have a sister and brother there. And from there we went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Bogeljic, do you still suffer from the injuries which were inflicted on you in the Motel Sretno in the night from the 18th May 1993 to the 19th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I have health problems. I've already said that my spine has been injured, I have a damaged kidney, and because of the sedatives, my digestive system has suffered too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And is -- are these problems the result of the beatings in the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Up until 1993, until the 18th of May -- I won't say I was an absolutely healthy person, but I had absolutely no injuries except for this right kidney, which I had a little problems with. But I had no haematoma on it or anything like that. I just had an inflammation of that kidney once, and that's why it was causing me some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogeljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the Prosecution's evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some small questions to clarify some answers that you gave. You explained at one point that a person brought you some water, cigarettes, and dates and that this person while you were detained indicated the reason why you had been arrested and beaten. Could you specify. Could you elaborate. What did this person tell you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: He said literally the following: "You should consider yourself lucky that your people have released some men --" I don't know who he meant, because the day before Marinko Benic had been killed in Catici, because of members of I don't know which unit. They had taken down the flag. The HVO tried to prevent it and killed him. And then the HVO captured some people. And then, if I understood him well, in order to have their soldiers released, they arrested us, but we were all civilians. That was what the man told me. I'm sorry I don't know his name, because he really helped us a lot. Once when they hit Mijo Petrovic with a bar, an iron bar that you use for beer crates, he jumped up and prevented this man from hitting him with it. The man was unconscious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question has to do with the point when after you were filmed by video. You were taken to be shown to three military men allegedly from the BH Army. And you said there was a French colonel there. What was he doing there? On what grounds are you saying that he was a colonel, that he was French, and he was a foreigner? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: This man -- I know this because after the conflict, after when Kakanj fell - for some people, it fell; for others, it was liberated. It depends on your point of view - I ended up in my parents' place. I was in bed. I couldn't move from my injuries. And then we went to Catici with my wife and son and I saw a man who the night before -- no, that's not right. On the 18th to the 19th I saw that same man at the sports field, and we thought it would be best to go to the UNPROFOR base. There were a lot of people there, and we entered, and that's how I managed to meet the colonel personally. An UNPROFOR unit was based there. They were supervising things. Actually, the meeting was organised because they wanted to reconcile the warring parties, even though there was no real war at the time. There were incidents, but not an out-and-out conflict yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that you showed your injuries before a representative of UNPROFOR and three soldiers from Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: And the HVO. And an interpreter was present too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you took your T-shirt off, no one said anything? When you showed them your injuries, there were no comments of any kind?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No. No. I don't remember any. Pavo said something though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were the only person to appear before these people. Were there others who appeared to show their injuries as well?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Only I was there before UNPROFOR, I and my wife. They said there was a meeting and can we see what happened, can we show the French colonel the injuries this person had sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted you to show your injuries to the French colonel, or to the BH soldiers, or to the colonel and the BH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I think they wanted know show my injuries to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence may now start its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Bogeljic. My name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to answer some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are some general questions I want to put to the question about the situation, since he worked in Kakanj and in Zenica, and this might be of significance for the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When answering questions put to you by the Prosecution, you said that in 1986 you graduated from the PTT school in Sarajevo and that you were qualified as a telecommunications engineer there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That same year you found a job in the post office in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You advanced rapidly, and you were soon made the chief responsible for maintaining the digital telephone exchange in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In 1993, I became the person responsible for the telecommunications centre. I was promoted by Kuc Harun, the director, because my former boss, Zoran Zekanovic, had left Zenica. He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already spoken -- you've already told the Prosecution about the conditions in that area in 1992, and I want to ask Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you whether in 1992 there were in fact no conflicts in Zenica between the Muslims and the Croats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, most of the Croats who were fit for military service joined the HVO because the HVO at the beginning also proclaimed that there would be a joint fight against the Serbian forces and the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, at the time the common enemy was the Serbian army and the JNA at the beginning. They had attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in fact the Serbian attacks directed at the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina made the population move and at the time a large number of Muslim and a smaller number of the Croatian population came to the area of Krajina? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And a lot of displaced persons arrived from Eastern Bosnia, Foca, Visegrad, Vlasenica, and Rogatica. On the whole, they were Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The number of refugees arriving in Zenica at the time was in the tens of thousands, not in the thousands; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The majority of those people arrived without any possessions, since they had been expelled from their homes and were not able to take anything with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the number of the population of Zenica towards the end of 1992 almost doubled.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I heard -- or in fact, I know that before the war in Zenica there were about 153.000 people, but my colleagues said that around 1993, when all these people arrived from other places, mainly Bosniaks, there were about 350.000 inhabitants. At least, that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But as you worked in Zenica and lived in Kakanj, you could notice, especially in Zenica, that at the beginning of 1993 some expelled people were coming to Zenica from the areas of Kiseljak, Busovaca, and Vitez; in fact, from areas that were under the control of the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All these people arrived and had been frustrated for various reasons. They said what had happened in Krajina, Eastern Bosnia, or the territories from which they had arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that up until the war, life in Zenica and Kakanj was a life that you lived on a daily basis, so people weren't distinguished on the basis of their religion or their ethnic membership. So you lived in a common manner. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you've partially answered this question when asked by the Prosecution: Is it correct to say that some of the politicians in fact abused, took advantage of the accident, this unfortunate event, and they tried to set the people against each other?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, even small children know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You and I know about that for sure, but perhaps the Trial Chamber isn't aware of this fact, so I have to ask you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you said that you worked in the Zenica PTT until March 1993, at which point you decided that it was no longer safe for you to go to work because a colleague had accused you of working for the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that I worked for the HVO. People working for telecommunications know a lot about communications, so my friends and I listened to what was happening, since we could listen to conversations and find out what was happening in the war areas. But no one was tapping any conversations for anyone, but it was in someone's interests to say that I was. My director, Kuc Harun, a very good man - we're even in contact now - he said, "Nenad, you know a certain person - I won't say who - said that you have done certain things. If I had called someone, you'd have been killed. You understand?"

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But your director didn't believe that and he supported you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Some didn't, but he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But that incident with your colleague in fact made you decide on your own that because you might not be safe you decided to leave your job and you informed your director of this decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I spoke to him and I said that I would leave for a while until things calmed down, because there were a lot of provocations in Zenica at the time. People would break into other people's flats and so on. People who lived in Zenica at the time were very well aware of these facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you went to Kakanj because you believed that the situation in Kakanj was far better than the situation in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
