utterances.text: There was no war in Kakanj. There were no refugees. And as you yourself have said, that contributed to the conflict and made people frustrated. People would arrive without any possessions. They had lost half of their families, et cetera. But it was still peaceful in Kakanj. I had a few Muslim neighbours whom I helped a lot. I knew people in Caritas and we would always help them. We would help them -- we'd help people from Ilijas and from Busovaca, but there was no one from Kiseljak or Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you can confirm that the tension - especially in Zenica, but even in Kakanj - had increased after people found out about the massacre in Ahmici and because of all the rumours that were heard after that event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And Geler, someone whom I have already mentioned, said, "Remember Ahmici. Babies were set on fire there." That's what he said when we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were questions put to you by the Prosecution too. And in order to better understand the situation of Kakanj, in Kakanj and in the area in which you lived, I have a few questions I want to ask you. Is it true to say that Kakanj is by the main road, which both before and even today connects Zenica and Sarajevo, but at the time - because part of the territory had been occupied by the Serbian forces - that part of the territory behind Visoko - it was no longer possible to use that road to get the Sarajevo? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But is it correct to say that it was nevertheless an important road between territories under the control of the BH Army? So from Visoko to Zepce?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only route they could use. They could only pass through by using that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that Kakanj, because of its economy, primarily because of its mine and hydroelectric -- and powerplant, it was very important for the army and for the HVO and for the either country?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that the strategic importance of Kakanj -- that it has strategic importance because you could connect not only territory under the control of the army but also territory under control of the HVO; for example, Busovaca, Kiseljak via Kakanj into Vares?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, yes. To Vares, yes, but not to Busovaca, because the surrounding hills were under the control of the army. We're talking about Busovaca, Vitez, and Kiseljak, in that direction. As far as I am aware, that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we only want to get an impression of the position Kakanj was in. Let's return to what you have already testified about. You said that when you stopped going to work in Zenica you started to do certain jobs for the HVO in March.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They needed someone who knew about telecommunications. I was the only person in Kakanj -- apart from the young men who worked in the post office, in the telecommunications section -- I was the only person who knew about these things in the HVO. They didn't have anyone who knew anything about telecommunications in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in March did you do some technical services for the HVO in Zenica as well in March?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: In March?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In March 1993.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Up until March, I went to the company to work every day. But whenever it was necessary to establish communications down there, I also controlled a certain area that I was responsible for. Topcic, Poljnemela [phoen], Lasva, in those centres, I did whatever was necessary for the BH Army and for others. That was my profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But when you returned to Kakanj - you have already said this, but I just want to repeat this because I don't know much about these technical matters - in fact you established those antennas and increased the radius of mobile telephones used by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Those telephones -- or rather, the HVO had its own telephones, in addition to the others. These were intended for the people who lived there. They would use these telephones. There was one in Kakanj by the primary school; one was in Caritas; another was to be in the village of Srijetes, so that the population could have communication, since the Croats -- most of the Croats had a lot of people who were living abroad. They did pay for it and the money went to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The network that you established from that point in time made it possible to use the communications, to use the communications network with Croatia, Slovenia, and the entire world.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: With the entire world, yes, that's correct. One such phone -- there was one such phone in Zenica, and later on in the post office they made this possible in the booths as well. But there was a mobile extension from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were involved in this work when you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No. Younger men did that. They would charge for this work. I only appeared when something needed to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I mean in a general sense, those responsibilities, those controls. You were responsible for that in May 1993 as well.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: In May 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You gave a detailed description of your arrest and being forcibly taken away. The people who arrived in the house of your mother-in-law, you didn't know them before, did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't find out who they were later on either.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Apart from one man. I found out about him because he introduced himself. And one man was with me three years ago. He told me what his name was. I knew his name was Serif, but I didn't know his surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When they arrested you, they didn't tell you which unit they were from, did they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No. I could only draw conclusions myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you didn't notice insignia of any particular kind on them, or did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I have already said. I said they had insignia of various kinds. It was 1993, and people would wear all sorts of insignia. But we who lived in Kakanj, we know that the 7th Muslim Battalion was in Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm saying that at the time you couldn't remember, you can't remember which of the patches from 1 to 24 these people had. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, I think they had the first one. But I also saw some wearing patches with the inscription "Allah-U-Ekber." And most of them had headbands with Arab words and they had a red band attached here, just like the kind of things people wear when they go into combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know it's difficult to remind you of these things and to remind you of events that relate to Motel Sretno, but you told the Prosecution that when you entered the area where the reception is located, you said that there were a number of soldiers there. You also said that you were already afraid of what was going to happen to you and you started justifying yourself, defending yourself.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason for which you didn't pay particular attention to the insignia that the troops who were present there had? Is it because of your fear that you didn't pay particular attention to this insignia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I didn't have time to look at what people had on their shoulders, but I saw certain things and I've told you about what I saw. One is too afraid in such situations. You have to experience these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The people you met in front of those rooms -- or rather, in the room in front of the reception area, you didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: I only knew one man who was from the neighbourhood. Unfortunately, that man died or he was killed. He was the local hodza. His name was Senada, I think. I saw him, him alone. But I didn't have time to look around me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were being maltreated there, they asked for you to give them money; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: On the whole, when I arrived they asked for money. First of all, they swear at you. They say they'll kill you, they'll cut your throat. That's what they did. But later I realised that the most important thing for them was to get money.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When at about 7.00 p.m. you were finally put into that third room, which is where you saw other people, they all told you that none of them had been beaten up until then.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: The people who were there -- I've already said that I couldn't see them very well at first, until my eyes got used to the dark. They were too afraid to say anything or to tell me anything. I only asked what the time was, and I know that someone told me that it was ten to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you were the first person to be beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. At least, I'm not aware of any other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The maltreatment that you all suffered continued until 3.00 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said, I think that it stopped about 3.00. About half past 3.00 they said someone would be turning up and then this officer appeared and said that there was some sort of misunderstanding. I don't remember everything, so take this with a grain of salt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were released in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Not exactly in the morning. It was around 12.00. I said 1.00 or 2.00. But it's difficult for me to remember. I was in a state of shock, after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Catici to your parents' house, you were visited by HVO representatives. Blasko Pavlovic was among them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He appeared. He wanted to know where some sort of a mobile phone was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was also interested in whether you had said anything about the HVO telecommunications network.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to say anything about that. All the inhabitants of Kakanj were aware of these matters, these communications devices, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But Blasko Pavlovic asked you whether when you were being maltreated you were asked about that subject.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No. He just came to visit me, to ask me how I was. That's all. It was just a formality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first time you gave a statement about what happened in the Motel Sretno was when you gave a statement to OTP investigators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, in Zagreb they asked me whether I wanted to give a statement or not. I didn't really feel like it, but in the end I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you didn't file any criminal charges against the people who had maltreated you, neither to the civilian nor the military police.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, there was no one I could turn to. The conflict had already broken out. The conflict broke out in a few days' time. A few days later the police force didn't exist. There was the military police force, various military police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of those complications, you didn't file a criminal report of any kind.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: No. I just went to see a doctor. They took some x-rays. It was Dr. Marin and Dr. Spasojevic who examined me. And there was another one who has died, another doctor. And they took some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to return to something that you mentioned to the Prosecution at the beginning of your testimony. At the beginning of 1993 in the area of Zenica and Kakanj, there were various armed groups. They had insignia of various kinds. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, BH Army brigades started being formed, is that correct? And the BH Army started being formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That process continued until you left Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I left Kakanj on the 11th of September. I think that at the time it was fairly peaceful in Kakanj. What had happened had happened. There was no longer a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you couldn't see as many armed groups who were present with insignia of various kind.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was a lot safer, both for the local population. My parents remained in Kakanj. But refugees were still arriving and creating problems. And people who would return from the battlefield in Vares. But neighbours and others, no, they didn't create any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that although you live in the Republic of Croatia you go to Kakanj very often; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to Zenica the too, and to the post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what I wanted to ask you as well. You often go to Zenica too?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: That's my town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have a lot of friends there.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Mostly Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You feel very safe among your friends both in Zenica and in Kakanj. You don't have problems of any kind.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Listen, there are always incidents. But there is one other thing that I haven't yet mentioned. I'll tell you about this because you're from that area. There are people who tried to protect me. And it was very hard for them when they realised what had happened to me, and they cried when I returned seven years later. Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But now when you go to Zenica and Kakanj, you go there without being afraid and you are completely safe, just like any other BH citizen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object against this line of questioning. That goes beyond the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at the beginning I said I would have some general questions, and the answers given by the witness today are answers that we frequently receive when responding to the Prosecution. I think it is very useful to hear what we have heard from the witness. I thank this witness, and I have finished my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now give the floor to the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bogeljic, on behalf of Mr. Kubura's Defence, I only have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said today during the examination that up until March you travelled almost daily from Kakanj to Zenica and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: If there was a bus running, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of your company was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the PTT company was based in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is in the centre of Zenica, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: Next to the Metalurg Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the headquarters of your company is in the immediate vicinity of the music school, about 100 metres away?

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't know where the music school in Zenica is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: The soldiers that took you on the 18th of May to the Sretno Motel were not wearing the insignia of the military police.

utterances.speaker: NENAD BOGELJIC
utterances.text: The military police? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn now towards the Prosecution. Has the Prosecution any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Withopf. Sir, you have answered the questions put to you both by the Prosecution and the Defence. You also answered several questions put by me. Therefore, your testimony and examination here is over. We thank you for coming and for testifying, and we wish you a safe journey home. I'm now going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem to deal with, and that is the admission into evidence of the CDs of this video. Do we have those CDs?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was informed 25 minutes ago that the CDs would be available within the next hour or sooner. Unfortunately, to this point in time we haven't the CDs yet. I would suggest that in the event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, there's something I don't understand. This piece of evidence is something that you communicated to the Defence counsel. We see that it is a videotape which was broadcast through our internal system. How is it possible that, knowing in advance, that you have produced this evidence but you don't have in your possession a copy which you could provide us with? When a document is produced, either a written document or a videotape, one has a copy for admission. And, however, you are telling me that you still don't have a copy. So technically I don't understand the difficulty that you are having right now. Could you explain why it is not possible to have those copies ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I certainly do understand your concerns, and I apologise for the late submission of such copies. However, the material which has been made available to the Defence on a CD contains a number of video -- the contents of a number of videotapes. The Prosecution gets such videotapes in the classical VHS format. What actually has to be done - and unfortunately, this takes a bit of time - the contents of the traditional videotapes have to be burned on a CD. The CDs that have been given to the Defence are not the very same CDs we are presenting and try to tender into evidence today. Again, the relevant portions of a two-hours' video - what it actually is, and we've seen, I think, some three or four minutes - have to be taken off and transferred from this one CD to the other CDs, and this takes, unfortunately, a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber now understands the technical problem involved, but it will always be possible to have it admitted maybe tomorrow at the beginning of the hearing. There's no urgency about it. We don't have to admit it in the next few minutes, because everyone has seen it. It is part of the record. So there's always time to admit it tomorrow. We can now go into private session because there's a minor issue to address, and it has to be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still on the subject of documents, I turn to the Prosecution. You have tendered a document. This was P50, a photo of the Sretno Motel. And you also produced another photograph, the photograph of the entry door where the witness told us that he entered through this door. But this document has not been officially tendered. Let us check. Let us check. Mr. Registrar, did we have a P51? I'm just checking. P50, yes, and P51. So that, too, is settled. We do have the exhibit numbers for these documents. So everything is in order now regarding the documents. It is 5.30. No more witnesses? I understand there was just one witness for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There was just one witness for today. And, Mr. President, Your Honours, the copies of the CDs just arrived, so I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wish to tender them into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's fine. Let us now admit these documents. If I understand well, each CD corresponds to one of the fragments that we saw. We saw several persons showing their injuries. And as far as I can recollect, there were three or four -- four. There were four. But let the Defence check. I think there were four persons that were filmed. So theoretically, we should have four CDs. I'm looking at the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, when you showed us the video clips, there were four persons filmed. If there were four persons, there should be four CDs. And it appears that we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please explain to us the two CDs so as to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's exactly the purpose, Mr. President, why I wish you to allow me to confer with the case manager, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're listening. The Defence also have in their hands two CDs, and they have an exhibit number, P52. The first says V000306, 1 of 2; and the other one says 2 of 2. Could you explain for us, please, what these are, what these two CDs correspond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on the two CDs is the full video sequence including the four portions that have been shown today in the course of the proceedings. We will provide the registrar, the Defence, and the Trial Chamber with an index actually indicating and detailing the relevant portion, which will enable you, Your Honours, and Defence to actually identify the respective portions of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, the two CDs contain the totality of the videos that last two hours. And on these two CDs we have the four persons that we saw. Is that right? So what you are tendering is not strictly limited to the four persons that we saw a moment ago but it covers the whole video material that was disclosed to the Defence before the beginning of trial. Could you explain that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we are tendering are only the portions which have been shown in the course of the today's proceedings, and the index we will provide the Trial Chamber and the Defence will exactly detail -- will exactly detail which portions mirror what we have seen in the course of the today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that for the purpose of legal security, it would be better for us to see these CDs once again, to avoid any confusion, because I really do not know what these correspond with. But Mr. Bourgon perhaps is going to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it's not that complicated. I think we should isolate the scenes that we saw in the courtroom. These should not contain anything other than what the Chamber has seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I believe too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution mentioned at the beginning that we received these documents on the 10th of October last year. We are not able at this point to confirm this. We didn't make any objections because we're going to verify our files this evening and perhaps tomorrow we can make some representations regarding those documents. Because at the moment we don't have those exhibits. We don't remember receiving them. But we will first verify our files before making any representations to the Chamber about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think the other Defence team is saying the same thing; right? Very well. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would say the same thing, that only the portions that are admitted into evidence should be before Your Honours and not the other material, which is not in evidence as yet. I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I turn again to Mr. Withopf. Have you understood the problem? It's not such a major problem, but it's there nevertheless. The Defence, quite rightly - and the Chamber shares their opinion - is telling us that we can admit today only what we saw a moment ago, and that is the video clips showing the four persons who showed their torsos. The ambiguity is that we have two CDs, so we don't know whether those two CDs contain solely those four persons or whether they contain other videos, and the Defence is telling us today that they think they had them in October but they can't confirm that that corresponds to what they saw in the courtroom, so they are asking for some time to reflect about it. So it would be better if we mark these for identification and we can come back to this, unless you are certifying that these two CDs contain solely and exclusively the four persons that we saw. So the solution would be to play them again, and we can verify. Perhaps we can do that, or maybe that's a technical problem, or we can wait until tomorrow, allowing you time to think it over and to verify that these tapes contain only images of the witness and the three other persons. What do you think about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, these two CDs contain two hours of video footage. It is the copy of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two hours. [In English] Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Exactly. It contains the copy -- the full copy -- of a videotape, one of these old-version-type videotapes which has been provided to the Prosecution in the course of the investigation. We tender only such portions into evidence which have been shown today. In order to enable to identify such portions, we will provide both the Trial Chamber and the Defence with an index that gives you the very exact times when the relevant portion starts and when the relevant portion ends. There is no ambiguity at the end of the day. If, however, Your Honours wish to isolate such portions from the CDs and to provide and to tender into evidence isolated portions, we can certainly do this as well; however, this takes again, unfortunately, a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Having examined and re-examined the Prosecution, the Chamber discovers that in fact these two CDs represent the totality of the video material and that they last two hours. And to solve the problem in connection with the testimony of the witness we had a moment ago, the Prosecution tells us that they can provide an index allowing us to find those passages. I think that the Defence is not agreeable at all with this method of procedure, and they would like us to admit only the clips and fragments relative to this witness which he authenticated. However, the Prosecution tells us that -- that if we so wish they could extract from this material only the fragments that we saw a moment ago. So I give the floor again to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We align ourselves to your suggestion. The sequences shown in the courtroom today should be the only ones admitted. This brings me to the question of documents received by the Defence -- disclosed to the Defence. We did receive CDs in the pre-trial period. However, we haven't checked whether those documents were part of the documents proposed by the Prosecution as documents that would be tendered into evidence, and that is what we are going to verify this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After deliberating on this technical issue, the Chamber decides, for the moment, to delay the admission of these two CDs which contain material which we haven't seen. And we would like to ask the Prosecution to extract from these CDs only the videos that we saw a moment ago. And then on the new CDs we will have only what was viewed and discussed a moment ago. In the meantime, the Defence is obviously going to review what was disclosed to it in October and check that they did have in their possession the sequences that we saw a moment ago. Therefore, I am returning to the Prosecution these two CDs. I prefer to have them replayed, reformed, reburnt. And so tomorrow we will have CDs which will contain only the sequences that we saw in the courtroom today. Surely this will not be too difficult, in view of the availability of resources. So this question of admission into evidence, what we saw will be regulated as soon as possible by the Prosecution, which will provide us on a single CD the four short clips relating to the witness and the three other persons. Having exhausted the agenda, it was time for the break anyway, but be will suspend the hearing until tomorrow, unless the Prosecution has something to say. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, can we please go in private session, since I have to make a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave and in accordance with the rule of the Pre-Trial Judge dated the 9th of November, 2001, I want to address the Trial Chamber in order to make an oral request to have permission for -- to respond to the response from the Prosecution, which was provided to our request asking the Trial Chamber to take judicial notice on the basis of previous cases. Seeing the time it is, I could make this oral request at the beginning of the hearing tomorrow, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about an order of the 9th of November. I don't have it before me. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order from the Pre-Trial Judge says that if one party wants to respond to the other side's response, they should ask to do that within a time limit of 20 days and they should mention the reasons for which it is necessary to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you have the time to make this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can do it immediately or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have the time, then we should deal with the matter immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In accordance with the Pre-Trial Judge's order, a party that wants to respond should ask the permission of the Trial Chamber if there are good grounds for such a response. The Prosecution provided a response to our request on the 26th of January, and this leaves us up until the 30th of January to ask for permission to respond. As the Trial Chamber suggests, we are addressing the Trial Chamber orally. If the arguments aren't convincing or sufficient, we could make this request in writing, within the four-day time limit if the Trial Chamber so decides. With regard to the grounds for our request for leave to respond - Mr. President, I refer to the response of the Prosecution on the 26th of January. To summarise the arguments put forward by the Prosecution with regard to this matter, the Prosecution presented three main grounds opposing our request: First of all, the relevance of the facts for which we are asking the Trial Chamber to take judicial notice; and secondly, considerations of public order, or rather, the possible negative consequences that it could have on the length of the proceedings if the Trial Chamber takes judicial notice of the facts that we are suggesting; and the third grounds put forward by the Prosecution concern the fact that the Defence, in its opinion, hasn't passed the test elaborated in the Krajisnik case. The test is referred to in paragraph 3 of its response. And they mention the criteria that have to be met so that the Trial Chamber may take judicial notice of certain facts. With regard to the first two grounds put forward by the Prosecution, first of all, the relevance of the facts, I think that the request and the response from the Prosecution would allow the Trial Chamber to rule on this subject. With regard to the second grounds put forward - that is to say, public order considerations or, rather, the possible negative consequences this would have for the length of the proceedings - I think that yet again, Mr. President, the facts presented by the Defence in its request, in its motion and by the Prosecution in its response are sufficient to allow the Trial Chamber to rule on this subject. We hope that we will have permission to respond on the basis of the third grounds, that is, the test put forward in the Krajisnik case. And this is the object of our request. We think we could facilitate the Trial Chamber's work by explaining, as suggested by the Prosecution, why all the criteria of the test elaborated in the Krajisnik affair -- case have been met, and this is -- it is on this basis that we are requesting that the Trial Chamber take judicial notice of certain facts. And this conclusion, Mr. President, we request permission to respond with regard to one of the main principles -- one of the main points put forward by the Prosecution. The facts that we are suggesting to the Chamber, we are stating that the criteria elaborated in the Krajisnik case should be respected. This is the important criterion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, what you are saying is that you are requesting leave to produce a response to the position adopted by the Prosecution with regard to the relevance, public order, and with regard to the test. So you would like to respond to that. We will give you our answer tomorrow at the beginning of the hearing at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having dealt with all the matters, I'll adjourn the hearing and we will resume our work tomorrow at 14.15.
